units.title: The replicated data-parallel memory baseline by dtype
outcomes: Derive replicated parameter, gradient and Adam state bytes from the tensors actually kept by a precision policy.
Separate persistent model state from gathered weights, activations, temporary buffers and allocator reserve.
units.why: Sharding savings are only meaningful against a stated baseline. Build on GPU memory: allocated, reserved, peak and memory models, and Optimizers from SGD to AdamW; here the new job is accounting by rank and dtype.

next.note: Partition the baseline without changing the update.

study.title: ZeRO: the model-state baseline
study.locator: arXiv:1910.02054v3, Section 3.1, Model States: Optimizer States, Gradients and Parameters; Section 3.2, Residual Memory Consumption

study.title: Memory usage revisited
study.locator: Zero Redundancy Optimizer (ZeRO), subsection Memory usage revisited
study.depth: Stop before ZeRO-1. Its extra FP32 accumulation buffer is a specific storage choice, not a mandatory extra copy under every mixed-precision implementation.

focus: For parameter count \(N\), sum each stored category once. The paper keeps half-precision parameters and gradients plus FP32 master parameters and two FP32 moments: \((2+2+4+4+4)N = 16N\) bytes.

FP32 parameters with FP32 gradients and two FP32 Adam moments also use \(16N\) tensor bytes, but have different lifetimes and communication payloads. Autocast alone does not require a persistent half-precision parameter copy.
Inspect Adam after its first update, when moments exist. Count per-parameter step scalars separately; gradients may be absent after clearing them.
Use decimal GB for \(10^9\) bytes and GiB for \(2^{30}\) bytes. Persistent model-state totals are not peak process or device memory.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, make a rank-local byte ledger for a model with \(N = 1{,}000{,}000\) parameters under the paper's half-precision Adam layout. Derive 16,000,000 tensor bytes per replica, excluding step scalars, activations and temporaries. Then count parameters, gradients and Adam moments in a small FP32 CPU model after one update and explain why its main tensor categories have the same total but a different layout.
traps: Counting an FP32 master parameter twice when the optimizer already updates the original FP32 parameter.
Dividing activations by world size while holding local microbatch fixed. ZeRO changes model-state ownership, not that local workload.
Measuring only before the first optimizer step and concluding that Adam has no state.

selfTest.q: Does BF16 compute imply two-byte persistent parameters?
selfTest.a: No. FSDP2 can keep original FP32 shards for the optimizer while gathering BF16 parameters for compute. State the storage policy separately from compute precision.

selfTest.q: Why is the paper's optimizer multiplier 12 rather than 8 bytes per parameter?
selfTest.a: It includes the four-byte FP32 master parameter as well as two four-byte Adam moments.

selfTest.q: Can a model whose persistent state fits still run out of memory?
selfTest.a: Yes. Activations, full gathered weights, full local gradients, communication staging, optimizer temporaries and allocator reserve can raise the peak above capacity.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the trainlab dtype-aware replicated-state ledger, checked against actual tensors after the first optimizer update.
units.stopWhen: Your ledger names every tensor category and reconciles its byte count with a small CPU model, without calling the persistent total a peak.

fit.note: The paper and Playbook locate the dtype baseline and residual memory; trainlab supplies the tensor-level accounting check.

units.title: ZeRO-1, ZeRO-2 and ZeRO-3 partitioning
outcomes: Derive per-rank model-state memory for ZeRO-1, ZeRO-2 and ZeRO-3 from ownership, including the unsharded floor.
Explain which rank updates each shard and how all ranks obtain the next parameter version.
Distinguish the assignment's whole-parameter optimizer partition from ideal evenly pooled sharding.
units.why: Each ZeRO stage removes a different replicated category. That distinction predicts both the memory floor and the communication needed to preserve data-parallel updates.

next.note: Turn ownership diagrams into a fully sharded step.

study.title: The three ZeRO stages
study.locator: Zero Redundancy Optimizer (ZeRO): ZeRO-1: Partitioning optimizer states; ZeRO-2: Adding gradient partitioning; ZeRO-3: Adding parameter partitioning (FSDP)
study.depth: Stop before Tensor Parallelism. Read the 'two times faster' aside as an equal-payload ring byte comparison, not a measured latency guarantee.

study.title: Ownership and memory savings
study.locator: arXiv:1910.02054v3, Sections 5.1 to 5.3, Deep Dive into ZeRO-DP; Figure 1 and Table 1

study.title: Optimizer-state sharding contract
study.locator: Section 6, problems `optimizer_state_sharding` and `optimizer_state_sharding_accounting`, printed pp. 37 to 38
study.depth: Implement the CPU correctness part now. For accounting parts (a) and (b), use a CPU tensor ledger first; with two or more GPUs, measure a model that fits your GPUs rather than requiring the handout's xl configuration.

focus: Let \(P\), \(G\) and \(O\) be total parameter, gradient and optimizer bytes, and \(R\) the rank count. Ideal even-shard persistent totals are \(P+G+O\), \(P+G+O/R\), \(P+(G+O)/R\) and \((P+G+O)/R\) for DDP through ZeRO-3.
In the paper's layout, \(P=2N\), \(G=2N\) and \(O=12N\). The advertised fourfold and eightfold stage-1 and stage-2 savings are large-degree limits, not exact savings at every rank count.

The assignment retains replicated parameters and gradients, updates only owned whole parameters, then broadcasts them. Its public test supplies matching gradients on both ranks; gradient averaging on disjoint data remains your trainer's responsibility.
Whole-parameter ownership, per-tensor dim-0 sharding, padding and pooled-byte ceilings are different allocation models. Write down which one your calculation uses.
units.reproduce: Derive the four memory expressions without looking. For the paper's layout with \(N=1{,}000{,}000\) and \(R=4\), obtain 16,000,000, 7,000,000, 5,500,000 and 4,000,000 persistent bytes per rank. Then draw which rank owns a parameter's moments, reduced gradient and stored weight at each stage; add the transient full weight needed by stage 3.
traps: Calling optimizer-state sharding gradient synchronization. Ownership of moments does not itself average different ranks' gradients.
Assigning tied parameter aliases to different owners and applying the update twice.
Using the ideal persistent ZeRO-3 total as an OOM prediction without a gather window.

selfTest.q: What memory floor remains as the rank count grows under ZeRO-2?
selfTest.a: The full replicated parameter storage. Gradients and optimizer state shrink ideally, but parameters do not.

selfTest.q: Does ZeRO-3 split a layer's matrix multiplication across the ranks?
selfTest.a: No. It splits stored model state; each rank gathers the required weights and computes on its own data. Tensor parallelism splits the layer computation.

selfTest.q: Why does the assignment need broadcasts after the optimizer step?
selfTest.a: Each owner changes only its parameters. Broadcasting those updates restores a consistent full parameter replica for the next forward on every rank.

selfTest.q: Do equal-payload reduce-scatter and all-gather always cost exactly the same as an all-reduce?
selfTest.a: Their total ring send volume equals a bandwidth-optimal ring all-reduce. Different dtypes, launch counts, topology, implementation and overlap can change elapsed time.

practice.name: TensorTonic: Account for ZeRO Memory by Stage
practice.note: Free. Public cases cover even four-way sharding, an uneven three-way byte pool and one rank. Follow its pooled-byte ceilings; they are not PyTorch's per-tensor allocation rule.

units.title: Parameter all-gather before compute and gradient reduce-scatter after backward
outcomes: Implement gather-before-use, release-after-use and reduced-gradient ownership in a tiny fully sharded trainer.
Match gradients and parameter updates to an unsharded oracle with the same global batch and loss normalization.
Explain when backward needs a full weight and when the optimizer needs only a shard.
units.why: Correct ownership is not enough if weights are absent when autograd uses them. This unit makes the parameter and gradient lifecycle explicit before adding scheduling optimizations.

next.note: Change the lifecycle while preserving the oracle result.

study.title: The current FSDP lifecycle
study.locator: How FSDP2 works and How to use FSDP2 / Model Initialization (page read 2026-10-14)

study.title: Build fully sharded training
study.locator: Section 7, problem `fsdp`, printed pp. 38 to 39; Section 8.3, equations (34) to (44), pp. 42 to 43
study.depth: Implement and test the CPU Gloo path first. Leave GPU profiling in `fsdp_accounting` to the peak-memory unit. The handout's FP32 master-weight prescription is its implementation contract, not a theorem forbidding other training formats.

focus: For a sharded linear layer, gather the full compute weight before forward. If released afterward, gather it again before backward computes input gradients. Reducing weight gradients does not replace that second gather.

Reduce-scatter combines contributions from all data ranks and gives each owner its reduced gradient slice. For equal local mean losses, divide the summed gradient by the data-parallel degree exactly once.
Resharding parameters normally means freeing the gathered representation and re-registering the stored shard. It is not another scatter collective.
The assignment shards Linear and Embedding weights and keeps norms replicated. Replicated parameters still need gradient synchronization. Build the optimizer against the parameters it must update.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, implement a tiny gather-compute-release-backward-reduce-scatter-update cycle on CPU Gloo. Use your DT-3 single-process oracle with identical initial weights, the concatenated global batch and equal local batch sizes. Record each rank's shard ranges and collective order; compare reconstructed gradients and several updates within explicit floating-point tolerances.
traps: Freeing a tensor still needed by autograd. The hook schedule and saved-tensor lifetime must agree; swapping storage blindly can corrupt backward.
Reducing only sharded weights while silently leaving replicated normalization gradients local.
Comparing each rank's local mean loss with the global mean and calling their difference an FSDP error. Reduce the metric separately.

selfTest.q: Why can a linear layer need its full weight during backward?
selfTest.a: Its input gradient multiplies the output gradient by the weight. Releasing the forward compute weight therefore requires restoring it before that multiplication.

selfTest.q: Is parameter resharding a network transfer?
selfTest.a: Not ordinarily. Each rank retains its persistent shard and frees the transient gathered copy. Gradient reduce-scatter is the network operation that produces the owned reduced gradient.

selfTest.q: When does a mean of local mean gradients equal the global mean gradient?
selfTest.a: When local losses use the same normalization and each rank has the same number of contributing examples or tokens. Unequal counts require weighting by those counts.

practice.name: CS336 Assignment 2: `fsdp`
practice.locator: Section 7; implement `get_fsdp`, `fsdp_on_after_backward` and `fsdp_gather_full_params` in `tests/adapters.py`; run `pytest tests/test_fsdp.py`
practice.note: Two CPU Gloo ranks. `test_fsdp_correctness` compares three SGD updates with full-batch training in FP32 and FP16 compute. `test_fsdp_gradient_sync` checks gradient shape and master dtype, and cross-rank agreement of replicated gradients. The section mini-project adds shard ownership and lifecycle evidence.

units.stopWhen: Your educational FSDP passes the public correctness and gradient tests, and its rank logs explain where each full weight and reduced shard lives.

fit.note: CS336 supplies the implementation contract and CPU public tests; the maintained tutorial supplies the current lifecycle vocabulary.

units.title: Reshard-after-forward policies and forward and backward prefetch
outcomes: Predict full-parameter lifetimes and gather counts for reshard-after-forward policies.
Compare prefetch depth using a live-state timeline and identify communication that remains exposed.
Explain the memory cost of keeping weights through backward or gathering future groups early.
units.why: A policy can save one gather yet retain a large full tensor. Prefetch can hide a gather yet create an OOM. Both choices need a lifecycle timeline, not a universal fastest setting.

next.note: Count the live windows and bytes introduced by each policy.

study.title: Reshard policy in PyTorch 2.14
study.locator: `fully_shard`, parameter `reshard_after_forward`; `FSDPModule.set_modules_to_forward_prefetch`, `set_modules_to_backward_prefetch` and `unshard`
study.depth: Read the Boolean and default policies first. Use the integer policy only in the simulator unless you have a suitable mesh; it needs a non-trivial divisor of the sharding degree.

study.title: Implicit and explicit prefetch
study.locator: Forward/Backward with Prefetching, including both timeline diagrams and explicit-prefetch code (page read 2026-10-14)

focus: With `reshard_after_forward=True`, discard the full weight after forward and gather it for backward. With `reshard_after_forward=False`, retain it until backward and avoid that gather.

In 2.14, `reshard_after_forward=None` resolves to true for non-root modules and false for the forward root. Set the policy explicitly when comparing schedules; do not assume a root-only run has two gathers.

Backward's default prefetch follows reverse post-forward order. An explicit list overrides it; deeper prefetch increases simultaneous gathered state and is only useful if earlier launch reduces waiting.

Use a deterministic event simulator first to measure live bytes and dependency stalls. With two or more GPUs, compare synchronized fixed-workload traces, allocated peaks and step times for these policies. CPU Gloo timings do not establish GPU overlap or interconnect performance.
units.reproduce: Draw a three-group forward/backward event trace twice: first release every group's full weights after forward, then retain them until backward. Assume each group needs its weight in both passes, no accumulation and no prefetch. Count two gathers per group in the first trace and one in the second; compute the simultaneous full-weight bytes. Add one-group-ahead prefetch and show the extra live window before testing the schedules in trainlab.
traps: Treating asynchronous launch as proof of overlap. Only a timeline with concurrent work and satisfied dependencies establishes overlap.
Copying a fixed prefetch list onto rank-divergent execution. Every group must still execute compatible collectives in the same order.
Using `unshard()` on the root and assuming it recursively gathers every nested FSDP group. It is not recursive.

selfTest.q: What does retaining full parameters after forward buy?
selfTest.a: It removes the backward parameter all-gather for those parameters, at the cost of a longer full-parameter lifetime. Gradient reduction is still required.

selfTest.q: Why can deeper prefetch make a previously fitting model fail?
selfTest.a: Several gathered groups and their staging buffers can coexist with current compute and saved activations. The persistent shards have not changed, but the live peak has.

selfTest.q: Why might the default keep the root's full parameters?
selfTest.a: The root is needed near the forward/backward boundary. Freeing and immediately gathering its parameters again can add traffic with little lifetime reduction. This is a heuristic, not proof that every root should be retained.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: trainlab event timelines for reshard and prefetch policies, with oracle checks and conditional multi-GPU traces.
units.stopWhen: Your policy comparison gives gather counts, peak live bytes and dependency stalls for identical work, and explains one case where more prefetch is worse.

fit.note: The tutorial's timelines and 2.14 API entries cover both policies at explain and measure depth; trainlab provides CPU simulation and conditional GPU evidence.

units.title: Flat parameters, wrapping granularity and hybrid sharding
outcomes: Explain FSDP1 flat storage, original-parameter views and communication grouping without treating them as FSDP2's representation.
Choose wrapping boundaries from the largest live group, launch count and shared-parameter ownership.
Map hybrid sharding's sharding and replication groups and explain both gradient reductions.
units.why: Wrapping determines what must fit in memory at once and which ranks communicate. Understanding both FSDP generations lets you read legacy code without importing its configuration into FSDP2.

study.title: Legacy flat parameters and hybrid sharding
study.locator: arXiv:2304.11277v2, Sections 3.2.1 Full Sharding, 3.2.2 Hybrid Sharding and 3.2.3 Autograd; Figures 3 and 4
study.depth: Read the representation and ownership design, not the paper's cluster benchmarks. This paper describes FSDP1.

study.title: From flat parameters to DTensor
study.locator: Why FSDP2? and FSDP1 <> FSDP2 API Differences, including the mesh and state-dict tables
study.depth: Use the tables for migration vocabulary only. The statements that forward prefetch is 'not yet implemented' or 'under discussion' are stale; use the 2.14 prefetch APIs from the preceding unit.

study.title: Current grouping and mesh contract
study.locator: Communication Grouping and Scheduling; `fully_shard` parameter `mesh` and the FSDP1 comparison

focus: FSDP1 flattens and concatenates a group's parameters, pads, then chunks the flat storage. Original parameter tensors are views into that storage. A handle manages this group's lifecycle; it is not a separate model-state category.
FSDP2 shards each parameter as a DTensor, normally along dim 0, but still groups communication by `fully_shard` calls. Per-parameter representation does not mean one collective per parameter.

Apply `fully_shard` bottom-up to blocks, then the root. The root owns remaining parameters such as embeddings and the output head. Root-only grouping materializes the whole model's managed weights together.

For a 2D hybrid mesh, the first dimension replicates and the second shards. Reduce-scatter within each shard group, then all-reduce matching gradient shards across replicas. Model-state memory scales with shard degree, not total world size.
units.reproduce: Draw a deterministic four-rank mesh with rows `[0, 1]` and `[2, 3]`. Identify sharding groups `[0, 1]` and `[2, 3]`, replication groups `[0, 2]` and `[1, 3]`, and each parameter shard's two copies. Sum gradient contributions within rows, then across columns; show that each owner obtains the same averaged shard as a global single-process oracle. Contrast root-only, per-block and per-linear communication groups on a two-block model.
traps: Dividing persistent memory by all four ranks in a two-by-two hybrid mesh. Each shard is replicated twice.
Wrapping tied aliases as unrelated groups. A shared parameter needs one compatible ownership and gather lifecycle for every use.
Assuming smaller groups always run faster. They lower individual gather sizes but increase collective launches and can expose latency.

selfTest.q: Does FSDP2 use a `FlatParameter` for each group?
selfTest.a: No. It stores per-parameter DTensor shards and groups them for communication. `FlatParameter` is the legacy FSDP1 representation.

selfTest.q: Why does hybrid sharding need a second gradient reduction?
selfTest.a: The reduce-scatter only combines data contributions inside one shard group. Matching shards in other replicated groups saw other data and must also be combined.

selfTest.q: What happens to parameters not assigned by the inner sharding calls?
selfTest.a: A later root call groups the remaining parameters. Omitting that call can leave intended-to-be-sharded parameters unmanaged.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the trainlab wrap-group inventory and four-rank hybrid ownership and reduction simulation.
units.stopWhen: You can reconstruct the hybrid reduction by hand, identify every group's parameters, and explain why your chosen granularity differs from both root-only and per-parameter grouping.

fit.note: The FSDP1 paper locates flat views and hybrid sharding; TorchTitan and the 2.14 API distinguish the current representation and grouping.

units.title: FSDP2 on DTensor with mixed parameter and reduction dtypes
outcomes: Apply FSDP2 bottom-up on a CPU device mesh and inspect local DTensor shards before and after a step.
Choose parameter, reduction and output dtypes separately and account for their storage and communication.
Construct the optimizer after sharding and verify global gradient clipping against an unsharded oracle.
units.why: Build on Precision formats, autocast and gradient scaling. The new issue is where casts occur across ranks: compute weights, reduction payloads and optimizer shards can have three different roles.

next.note: Test precision and ownership failures independently.

study.title: FSDP2 precision and DTensor optimizer
study.locator: Enabling Mixed Precision; Gradient Clipping and Optimizer with DTensor; revisit Model Initialization's DTensor inspection (page read 2026-10-14)

study.title: MixedPrecisionPolicy in PyTorch 2.14
study.locator: `MixedPrecisionPolicy`: `param_dtype`, `reduce_dtype`, `output_dtype` and `cast_forward_inputs`; `fully_shard` user contract

focus: Start with FP32 and a 1D CPU mesh on Gloo. Shard blocks before the root, use `model(x)` so hooks run, then construct AdamW from the sharded parameters. Inspect global shapes and `to_local()` separately.

For original FP32 parameters, `MixedPrecisionPolicy(param_dtype=torch.bfloat16, reduce_dtype=torch.float32)` gathers BF16 weights, computes in BF16 and reduces gradients in FP32. The optimizer updates original FP32 shards; it does not need another FP32 master copy.
If `reduce_dtype=None` and `param_dtype` is set, reduction uses the compute dtype. `output_dtype` changes floating-point outputs at the module boundary, not the optimizer's state dtype.

Use `torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_` on the DTensor parameters, not on each rank's local shards separately. A global norm must combine the disjoint gradient contributions without counting replicated copies twice.
units.reproduce: Adapt the tutorial to two CPU Gloo processes with `init_device_mesh('cpu', (2,))` and a tiny two-linear-layer model. First match several FP32 AdamW updates and a clipped gradient norm to the single-process global-batch oracle. Then use BF16 parameter compute and FP32 reduction; inspect the full compute weight during a forward pre-hook, the FP32 shard and gradient after backward, and FP32 Adam moments after the update. Compare mixed precision to an oracle with matching casts, not to a bitwise FP32 target.
traps: Inspecting the weight in a post-forward hook registered after FSDP's hook and expecting the compute dtype. It may already have been resharded to the original dtype; inspect inside forward or after FSDP's pre-hook.
Passing `model.forward(x)` directly and bypassing the gather hooks.
Clipping each local shard to the same maximum norm. That implements different scaling from clipping the reconstructed global gradient.

selfTest.q: Which dtype determines parameter all-gather bytes?
selfTest.a: The unsharded parameter dtype, selected by `param_dtype` when set. The stored optimizer shard can remain FP32.

selfTest.q: Does FP32 reduction recover precision lost during BF16 compute?
selfTest.a: No. It limits additional rounding during reduction, but cannot recover information already lost in low-precision computations.

selfTest.q: Why initialize the optimizer after `fully_shard`?
selfTest.a: It must reference the DTensor parameters that the sharded optimizer step will update, with the correct ownership and shape semantics.

selfTest.q: What should happen when a correct mixed-precision run is compared with FP32?
selfTest.a: Small numerical differences can occur. Validate against a same-policy oracle with explicit tolerances, and report any FP32 comparison as a precision comparison rather than bitwise equivalence.
